title: Gadgadasvara (Kern ch. 23)
hookLine: a bodhisattva who appears in many forms to help

cards: Before the visitor arrives, flowers arrive. Lotuses made of jewels appear on Vulture Peak, near where the Buddha is teaching, and the bodhisattva Manjushri asks what they mean.
Someone is coming, the Buddha says, from a far-off world: a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara.
And before he sets out, his own Buddha gives him a piece of travel advice that would do anyone good, on any trip, to any place that looks rougher than home.

teach.b: First, the visitor. Gadgadasvara lives in a radiant world far away, and he himself is vast and shining. He wants to come and see Shakyamuni and the bodhisattvas around him, and hear this teaching.

teach.h: DON'T LOOK DOWN ON THAT WORLD.
teach.b: His own Buddha tells him, in effect: when you go there, don't look down on that world. It is uneven, with hills and rough ground, and the beings there, even its Buddha and bodhisattvas, are small next to you.
Don't think less of them for it. The sutra imagines our world from the outside, finds it bumpy and modest, and makes respect the visitor's first instruction. Third, the forms.

When he arrives, a bodhisattva in the assembly asks what this visitor has done to be so radiant. The Buddha answers, then adds something more: this bodhisattva has taught the sutra in many forms. As Brahma and as Indra.

teach.h: A KING, A MERCHANT, A CHILD.
teach.b: As a king, a merchant, a householder. As a monk or a nun, a layman or a laywoman, a boy or a girl. Even among beings in the hardest realms.
Whatever form would let someone hear, that is the form he takes.
Fourth, the thread back. This is the skillful means from the start of the sutra, now walking around in a body. The teaching doesn't wait for people to come to its shape; it takes theirs.
And in Kumarajiva's Chinese, the visitor's name is Wonderful Sound.

how: In East Asian Buddhism this bodhisattva is known by the Chinese name Wonderful Sound, and the chapter is studied as a teaching on skillful means, the many forms a bodhisattva takes to help.

o: a heavenly musician who plays for the Buddha's crowd
a visitor bodhisattva who teaches in whatever form will be heard
a far-off Buddha who never leaves his radiant world

p: announce the visitor on the peak
don't look down on that world
a king, a merchant, a child
some of the forms he takes

s: Gadgadasvara's Buddha tells him our world is as radiant as his own
he says it is uneven and its beings small, and tells him not to look down on it.
the chapter says he has taught in the forms of monks, nuns, lay people and children
whatever form lets someone hear, that is the form he takes.
the bodhisattva teaches only in one fixed form
the chapter lists many forms, from gods to children.

games.q: you are a radiant bodhisattva about to visit a rough, uneven world where everyone is small next to you. what does your own Buddha tell you before you go?
o: dazzle them, so they look up to you
don't look down on that world or its beings
stay only long enough to be polite
games.why: the first instruction is respect: don't think less of that world, its Buddha or its bodhisattvas because they are small.

practice: Let one person come to mind who might need some help this week, and ask gently: what form would help actually take for them?
Maybe a listener, maybe someone who fixes the leaky thing, maybe someone who leaves them in peace for an afternoon. Let the answer come, even if it isn't the role you like playing best.

wordCard.voice: Gadgadasvara. In the Lotus Sutra, a bodhisattva from a far-off world who teaches in whatever form will let someone hear, and is told not to look down on ours. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the bodhisattva's name; svara means voice or sound. The Chinese calls him Wonderful Sound.

carryVoice: Your line: many forms. Help takes the shape of the one being helped. See you tomorrow.
